# Least squares estimation

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The simplest idea: minimise the distance

For each day, take the gap between what we observed and what the model predicts, square it, and add the squares up

$$\text{SSE} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \bigl(y_i - f(t_i, \theta)\bigr)^2$$

- $y_i$ is the observation on day $t_i$
- $f(t_i, \theta)$ is what the model predicts for that day with parameters $\theta$

The parameters that make this sum smallest are the [least squares estimates]{style="color: tomato;"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Why square the errors?

- Squaring makes every gap positive, so gaps above and below the curve do not cancel
- Big misses are punished much more than small ones
- The sum is smooth in $\theta$, which the optimisers we are about to use rely on
- If the errors were normally distributed with the same variance everywhere, least squares would be the maximum likelihood answer

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### What the squares do not know

- A single outlier can pull the whole fit towards itself
- Every day counts the same, whether 3 pupils were in bed or 300, which is rarely how counts behave
- The number that comes out has no probability attached to it

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What least squares gives you

- An answer in seconds, with algorithms that have been around for two centuries and are in every piece of software
- A method everyone in the room can explain to everyone else
- A good starting point for the methods that follow, which is how we will use it in the next section

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What it does not give you {.smaller}

- Any measure of how sure we are: the valley in the landscape was clearly tilted and wide, and the estimate says nothing about that
- A way to compare two models that both fit reasonably well
- A justification for treating every day the same way, when the counts plainly vary more at the peak than in the tails

------------------------------------------------------------------------
